records.text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Moab, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they burned the bones of Idumea’s king into lime.

Josiah turned aside and saw the tombs there in the city. He sent and took the bones from the tombs, burned them on the altar, and defiled it, according to the Lord’s word which the man of God spoke while Jeroboam stood at the festival beside the altar. Turning, he lifted his eyes toward the tomb of the man of God who had spoken these words.
He said, ‘What is that rocky marker I see?’ The city’s men told him, ‘It is the man of God who came out of Judah and proclaimed these words which he proclaimed against Bethel’s altar.’
He said, ‘Leave it alone. Let no one move his bones.’ His bones were spared together with the bones of the prophet who came from Samaria.
I will send fire upon Moab, and it will devour the foundations of her cities. Moab will die in weakness, with shouting and the sound of a trumpet.
I will kindle fire upon Rabbah’s walls, and it will devour her foundations with shouting on the day of war; she will be shaken on the day of her end.

Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of the sons of Judah, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they rejected the Lord’s law and did not keep His ordinances. Their vain things, which they made, led them astray—the things their fathers followed.

They did not keep His testimonies by which He warned them. They followed vain things and became vain, and followed the nations around them, concerning whom He had commanded them not to do such things.
They abandoned the commandments of the Lord their God. They made a casting for themselves, two heifers, made groves, bowed down to all heaven’s host, and served Baal.
I will send fire upon Judah, and it will devour Jerusalem’s foundations.”

And if you do not listen to Me to consecrate the Sabbath day, not lifting burdens and not entering Jerusalem’s gates on the Sabbath day, I will kindle fire in her gates, and it will devour Jerusalem’s quarters and not be extinguished.
Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they sold a righteous person for silver and a poor person for sandals,
to acquire the poor with silver and a lowly person in exchange for sandals? And we will trade from every kind of produce.”

But I removed the Amorite from before them, whose height was like a cedar and who was strong as an oak. I removed his fruit above and his roots below.
Below, his roots will dry up; above, his harvest will fall.
I brought you up from Egypt’s land and led you around in the wilderness forty years, to inherit the Amorites’ land.

And you shall remember all the way wherein the Lord your God led you in the wilderness, to afflict you and to test you, that the things in your heart might be known, whether you would keep His commandments or not.

And He afflicted you, and made you hunger, and fed you with manna, which your fathers did not know, that He might declare unto you that man shall not live by bread alone, but man shall live by every word that proceeds through the mouth of God.
Your garments did not wear out upon you, neither did your feet become calloused; behold, these forty years.

triples.relationship: contrast in the burning of human bones
triples.rationale: Amos condemns Moab for burning the bones of Idumea's king into lime. Kings describes Josiah burning bones from tombs upon Bethel's altar to defile it, according to the Lord's word, while sparing other bones. The physical action is related, but its purpose and assessment differ sharply between the passages.

triples.relationship: repeated pairing of fire and war shouting in distinct national oracles
triples.rationale: The Moab judgment combines fire consuming city foundations with weakness, shouting and trumpet sound. The Rabbah judgment combines fire consuming foundations with shouting on the day of war. Their repeated fire-and-shouting combination connects the separate national judgments, while the trumpet is particular to Moab's unit.

triples.relationship: parallel rejection of divine commands and pursuit of vain things
triples.rationale: Amos accuses Judah of rejecting the Lord's law, failing to keep His ordinances and being led astray by vain things. Kings describes Israel failing to keep His testimonies, following vain things and abandoning His commandments. The two-part indictment closely corresponds across the differently identified peoples.

triples.relationship: parallel divine fire consuming Jerusalem's buildings
triples.rationale: Amos announces fire in Judah consuming Jerusalem's foundations. Jeremiah conditionally warns of fire in Jerusalem's gates consuming her quarters if the people do not consecrate the Sabbath. The Lord's fire upon the same city's structures connects them; Jeremiah supplies the particular Sabbath condition.

triples.relationship: repeated trading of vulnerable people for silver and sandals
triples.rationale: The earlier accusation names the righteous sold for silver and the poor for sandals. The later commercial speech names acquiring the poor for silver and the lowly for sandals. The repeated forms of payment make the connection particular, while selling and acquiring describe different sides of exploitation.

triples.rationale: Amos describes fists upon poor people's heads and turning aside the way of the humble. Isaiah condemns turning aside the poor's judgment and seizing the needy people's justice. Oppression and the turning-aside language connect them; Isaiah explicitly focuses on legal judgment.

triples.relationship: related use of oppressively acquired goods in a sacred setting
triples.rationale: Amos places drinking wine from extortions in the house of their God. Malachi criticizes bringing things seized by force among the sacrifices. Both associate goods gained through wrongdoing with a sacred setting; Amos describes drinking and does not explicitly call the wine a sacrifice.

triples.relationship: parallel ruin of roots below and produce above
triples.rationale: Amos describes removing the Amorite's fruit above and roots below. In Bildad's speech, roots dry up below and the harvest falls above. The paired vertical image expresses comprehensive ruin, with national judgment in Amos and the account of the unjust in Job's surrounding speech.

triples.relationship: shared recollection of divine guidance through forty wilderness years
triples.rationale: Amos recalls God bringing Israel from Egypt and guiding them forty years in the wilderness to inherit the Amorite's land. Deuteronomy recalls the Lord's wilderness guidance, feeding and the forty years. The period and divine guidance connect them, with inheritance emphasized in Amos and testing and instruction in Deuteronomy.

triples.rationale: Amos recalls God raising prophets from the people's sons, alongside young men for consecration. Deuteronomy promises a prophet raised by the Lord from among their brothers. The divine raising and origin within the people connect the prophetic callings, while number and temporal setting differ.

triples.relationship: parallel failure of military strength to save
triples.rationale: Amos says the strong will not retain strength and the fighter will not save his life, alongside failed flight. The psalm says a king is not saved by a great force and a giant is not saved by abundant strength. Both deny rescue through martial capacity, with different representative figures.

triples.relationship: related failure of confidence associated with horses
triples.rationale: Amos includes the horse rider among those who will not save their lives. The psalm calls a horse false for salvation and says its abundant power will not save it. The specific horse-and-salvation pairing connects the warnings, while Amos explicitly focuses on the rider.
